questions.question: An email from 'IT Support' says your mailbox is full and you must click a link to confirm your password. What should you do first?
options: Click the link and enter your password so your mailbox keeps working
Reply to the sender asking them to prove they are genuine
Report the message as phishing and contact IT through a known, separate channel
Forward it to colleagues so everyone is aware
questions.explanation: Urgency plus a request for credentials is the classic phishing pattern. Report it with the phishing button and verify through a channel you already trust - never by replying or clicking the link.

questions.question: Which unexpected email attachment should make you most suspicious?
options: A holiday photo saved as .jpg
An executable or compressed archive (.exe or .zip) you were not expecting
A meeting invitation in your calendar
A PDF invoice from a supplier you know
questions.explanation: Executables and archives are common malware carriers. Even files that look harmless, such as PDFs, should be verified when unexpected - but a surprise .exe or .zip is a major red flag.

questions.question: What makes spear phishing more dangerous than a generic phishing email?
options: It is always sent from a government address
It is researched and personalised for a specific person or team
It only targets people without antivirus software
It never contains links or attachments
questions.explanation: Spear phishing uses real names, projects and context gathered from social media or previous breaches, making the request far more convincing. Verify unusual requests through a second channel.

questions.question: Someone in a courier uniform tries to follow you through a secure door without swiping a badge. What is the best response?
options: Hold the door open - the uniform proves they are legitimate
Politely challenge them and direct them to reception to be signed in
Ignore them and walk on quickly
Take their parcel and let them wait outside
questions.explanation: Tailgating bypasses every access control you have. A friendly challenge and a redirect to reception is not rude - it is exactly what a security-aware organisation expects.

questions.question: An attacker invents a believable scenario - such as an urgent audit - to manipulate you into revealing information. What is this technique called?
options: Pretexting
Patching
Port scanning
Phishing simulation
questions.explanation: Pretexting is a fabricated story used to establish trust and justify an unusual request. The defence is to verify identity and authority through an independent channel.

questions.question: Why is reusing the same password across multiple services dangerous?
options: It makes your keyboard wear out faster
A breach at one service can be used to access all your other accounts
Websites automatically share passwords with each other
It slows down your internet connection
questions.explanation: Attackers replay stolen username and password pairs against other services - credential stuffing. One breach then becomes many. Every account needs its own unique password.

questions.question: Which of these is the strongest password approach?
options: P@ssw0rd! - it has symbols and numbers
The same long random password everywhere
A long unique passphrase for each account, stored in a password manager
Your pet's name plus your birth year
questions.explanation: Length and uniqueness beat complexity tricks. A password manager lets you use a different long passphrase for every account without memorising them all.

questions.question: Where should you store your work passwords?
options: In a spreadsheet on your desktop
In a note taped inside your desk drawer
In an approved password manager
In your browser's autofill with no master password
questions.explanation: Use the password manager approved by your organisation. Spreadsheets and notes are easily copied, and an unprotected browser store is trivial to extract from a stolen device.

questions.question: What does multi-factor authentication (MFA) add to a password?
options: A second password that must be different
An additional proof of identity from a different category, such as a device or biometric
A longer password expiry period
A backup email address
questions.explanation: MFA combines something you know with something you have or are - for example a password plus an authenticator code or security key. A stolen password alone is then not enough.

questions.question: Which second factor is generally the most resistant to phishing?
options: A code sent by SMS
A code sent to your email
A hardware security key using FIDO2/WebAuthn
A security question about your first school
questions.explanation: Hardware security keys bind the login to the real website origin, so a fake login page cannot reuse the response. SMS and email codes can be intercepted or relayed.

questions.question: Your phone receives five MFA approval prompts you did not initiate. What should you do?
options: Approve one so the prompts stop
Ignore them and wait for them to expire
Deny them and report the activity - someone may already know your password
Turn your phone off and say nothing
questions.explanation: This is MFA fatigue or push bombing. Repeated prompts mean an attacker has your password and is trying to wear you down. Deny, report to IT, and change your password.

questions.question: You suspect a file server is infected with ransomware. What is the safest first step?
options: Disconnect it from the network and report it to IT security immediately
Restart it several times to see if the problem clears
Move important files to a USB drive
Pay the ransom quickly to get the files back
questions.explanation: Containment comes first. Isolating the device limits encryption and spread, and preserves evidence. Do not move files to removable media - you may carry the malware with them.

questions.question: Which backup approach best protects an organisation from ransomware?
options: One copy on a network drive mapped to every PC
Offline or immutable backups that are regularly tested for restore
A copy in the same server room as the live data
Weekly screenshots of important folders
questions.explanation: Ransomware hunts for connected backups. Offline or immutable copies, tested regularly, are the reliable way back. The 3-2-1 rule - three copies, two media types, one off-site - is a useful guide.

questions.question: Why should you avoid enabling macros in a document received unexpectedly?
options: Macros make the document too large to email
Macros can run code that installs malware
Macros stop the document from printing
Macros are only available to administrators
questions.explanation: Office macros are a well-used route for delivering malware, including ransomware. Treat any 'enable content' prompt on an unexpected document as a warning sign.

questions.question: An email appears to be from your CEO asking you to buy gift cards urgently and keep it confidential. What should you do?
options: Buy the cards - it is the CEO
Reply to the email asking for confirmation
Verify the request with the CEO or a second manager using a known phone number
Forward the email to a colleague and ask them to handle it
questions.explanation: Urgency, secrecy and unusual payment methods are business email compromise hallmarks. Reply-to verification fails because the attacker controls the mailbox. Call a known number instead.

questions.question: A supplier emails to say their bank details have changed. What is the correct action?
options: Update the payment details and pay the next invoice
Call the supplier on a previously known number to verify the change
Reply to the email and ask them to confirm the new account
Wait until the next invoice arrives and check the logo
questions.explanation: Payment-diversion fraud relies on you trusting the email itself. Verify using contact details you already hold, not the phone number or reply-to address in the suspicious message.

questions.question: What does the principle of least privilege mean?
options: Everyone should have administrator rights so they can fix problems
People should only have the access they need for their current role
Access should be reviewed once every five years
Only senior managers may use email
questions.explanation: Least privilege limits the damage a compromised account or malicious insider can do. Access should be granted for a clear purpose and removed promptly when no longer needed.

questions.question: Under UK GDPR, how long do organisations generally have to report a serious personal data breach to the regulator?
options: 24 hours
72 hours
30 days
There is no time limit
questions.explanation: Where a breach is likely to result in a risk to people's rights and freedoms, the organisation must notify the regulator without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware.

questions.question: Which of these is personal data?
options: A company's public website address
A customer's name, home address and order history
The model of a office printer
A generic support mailbox address
questions.explanation: Personal data is information relating to an identified or identifiable living person. Names, addresses and purchase history all count and must be handled lawfully and securely.

questions.question: Which control best defends against invoice or mandate fraud?
options: Paying suppliers faster to avoid complaints
Verifying any change of bank details by calling a known contact
Using a shared finance mailbox for all payments
Relying on the supplier's email signature
questions.explanation: Mandate fraud succeeds when a convincing email changes payment details. An independent callback to a number you already hold breaks the attack chain.

questions.question: An online investment offer promises guaranteed high returns if you act within the hour. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A legitimate limited-time offer
A scam using urgency and unrealistic returns
A normal bank promotion
A government savings scheme
questions.explanation: Guaranteed high returns and time pressure are classic investment fraud signals. Genuine investments carry risk and never need an instant bank transfer to a stranger.

questions.question: You need to check your bank account while using public Wi-Fi in a cafe. What is the safest option?
options: Use the cafe Wi-Fi - it is password protected
Use your mobile data or a trusted VPN instead
Ask another customer to log in for you
Disable your device password to speed things up
questions.explanation: A café password is shared with everyone in the room and says nothing about the network's safety. Mobile data or a trusted VPN avoids untrusted networks for sensitive activity.

questions.question: Why is posting real-time holiday photos on social media a security risk?
options: It uses too much mobile data
It publicly advertises that your home is empty and reveals your location
It makes your phone battery drain faster
It can damage your camera
questions.explanation: Criminals use social media to time burglaries and to build convincing social engineering stories. Share the trip afterwards, and review your privacy settings.

questions.question: Why should you install operating system and software updates promptly?
options: They change the wallpaper automatically
They fix known security vulnerabilities that attackers actively exploit
They make your device run slower on purpose
They are only needed for new devices
questions.explanation: Updates close vulnerabilities that are often public and actively exploited within days. Delaying updates leaves a known door open. Enable automatic updates where possible.

questions.question: Your work phone is lost. What should you do first?
options: Wait a few days in case it turns up
Report it immediately so it can be located, locked or wiped remotely
Change your wallpaper from another device
Post about it on social media
questions.explanation: Fast reporting limits access to email, files and saved credentials. Device encryption and a screen lock are your safety net, but they do not replace reporting.

questions.question: An employee who is leaving asks to copy the customer database 'for reference'. What is the correct response?
options: Allow it - they built the database
Refuse, explain the policy and report the request through the proper channel
Copy it for them yourself
Send it to their personal email to avoid arguments
questions.explanation: Departing staff are a recognised data-loss risk. Access should be removed on schedule, and requests for bulk copies should be refused and reported, not negotiated informally.

questions.question: A colleague asks to borrow your login to finish a task while you are on leave. What should you do?
options: Share your password - it is only for one day
Write the password on a sticky note for them
Never share credentials; arrange delegated access with the right permissions
Let them use your session while you watch
questions.explanation: Shared accounts destroy accountability and are a gift to insider threats. Use proper delegation so actions are attributable and limited to what the task needs.

questions.question: You receive a text saying a parcel is waiting and asking you to click a link to pay a small fee. What should you do?
options: Click the link - the fee is tiny
Reply with your card details
Do not click; check the delivery through the courier's official app or website
Forward it to friends to warn them
questions.explanation: Smishing uses small payments and curiosity to harvest card details. Navigate to the courier yourself rather than trusting the link, and report the message.

questions.question: You find a USB drive in the office car park. What should you do?
options: Plug it into your laptop to see who owns it
Hand it to IT or security without connecting it
Take it home and format it for personal use
Try it on a colleague's computer first
questions.explanation: Dropped USB drives are a classic way to deliver malware - sometimes called baiting. Never connect unknown media. Give it to IT so it can be handled safely.

questions.question: Which combination gives the strongest everyday protection for a work account?
options: A short password changed every week
A unique long passphrase plus phishing-resistant MFA
Antivirus alone
Using the same password as your personal email
questions.explanation: A unique long passphrase defeats credential reuse and brute force, while phishing-resistant MFA blocks most account takeover even if the password leaks. Layer both.
